name: Liavex
description: Liavex is an oxytocin-vasopressin SNT-pathway amplifier that deepens trust, affection, and social bonding between individuals who take it in proximity to one another. It accelerates the neurological processes of attachment, making people feel rapidly and genuinely close to those around them during the dose window. Lazarus markets two versions: LiavexPro for corporate team-building and leadership programs, and LiavexIntimate for couples and relationship counseling.
effects: Rapid deepening of trust and affection toward people in proximity
Reduced social guardedness and defensive behavior
Increased willingness to share personal information and vulnerability
Genuine feelings of warmth and attachment — not artificial euphoria
Enhanced ability to read and respond to others' emotional states
side_effects: Bonding is non-selective — users bond with whoever is present, not necessarily intended recipients
Post-dose attachment that may not reflect actual compatibility or values
Exploitation risk: bonds formed under Liavex can be leveraged by those who did not take it
Emotional whiplash when bonded feelings fade after dose — grief-like response
Corporate misuse: employees bonded to managers via Liavex show increased compliance and reduced willingness to report misconduct
Long-term couples use linked to codependency and inability to resolve conflict without re-dosing
cultural_context: Liavex is one of the most ethically debated pharmaceuticals in legal circulation. Its corporate use — in team retreats, onboarding programs, and leadership seminars — is widespread but quietly controversial. Employees often don't know it's been included in catered food or beverages at company events. In relationships, couples counselors are split: some use it as a legitimate therapeutic tool to rebuild connection; others refuse to prescribe it, arguing that bonds formed under its influence are not informed consent. On the street, it's called 'the Tie' and is used in seduction, manipulation, and — at its darkest — coercion. There is no law distinguishing consensual Liavex use from its administration without knowledge.
story_hooks: A player character realizes, in retrospect, that Liavex was served at a corporate onboarding event they attended six months ago. The warm loyalty they've felt toward their employer ever since — the reason they haven't reported what they've seen — may not be entirely their own.

A Tier 4 divorce attorney has a client whose spouse has been micro-dosing Liavex into their morning coffee for two years. The client is devastated and furious — but there is currently no law making this a crime, only a civil matter.

Someone on the Shelf is selling Liavex-laced street food near a transit hub — bonding desperate, isolated people to a charismatic figure who is building something. Whether it's a community or a cult depends on who's asking.
